title: ANGEL FOUNDERS TRANSFER MORE THAN 10 MILLION SUPER-VOTING SHARES TO ANGEL MISSION TRUST TO PRESERVE COMPANY’S MISSION FOR GENERATIONS
summary: Angel (NYSE: ANGX) – a media and technology company successfully pioneering a first of its kind audience-driven studio model in which Angel Guild members wat...
body_text: ANGEL FOUNDERS TRANSFER MORE THAN 10 MILLION SUPER-VOTING SHARES TO ANGEL MISSION TRUST TO PRESERVE COMPANY’S MISSION FOR GENERATIONS Provo, UT—July 2, 2026 Angel (NYSE: ANGX) – a media and technology company successfully pioneering a first of its kind audience-driven studio model in which Angel Guild members watch, screen and vote on which films and television series get distributed in theaters and on the Angel platform – today announced that Angel Co-Founders Neal Harmon and Jeffrey Harmon have irrevocably transferred more than 10 million shares of super-voting class B Angel stock to the Angel Mission Trust. This creates a perpetual stewardship structure that preserves the company’s independence, values, and mission to amplify light for generations to come. As Angel Guild members vote, they pledge to choose excellent entertainment that is true, honest, noble, just, authentic, lovely, admirable, or joyful. This is what it means to amplify light. “Our heroes are the Disney brothers,” said Neal Harmon, Angel Co-Founder and CEO, “And while Disney still has an amazing heritage, we’ve all watched the company’s mission drift after Walt and Roy were gone. Our hope is that this Trust will help Angel’s mission last long after we are gone.” The Trust draws inspiration from mission-driven companies such as Patagonia, Hershey, and Rolex. It is irrevocable, with a professional Trustee, independent Enforcer, and Trust Stewardship Committee. All decisions prioritize generational mission integrity and long-term performance over short-term gains. Angel will continue to innovate through its pioneering Angel Guild model while the Angel Mission Trust provides enduring governance. About Angel Studios, Inc. Angel (NYSE: ANGX) is a media and technology company successfully pioneering a first-of-its-kind audience-driven studio model. Founded by brothers who struggled to find films they could watch with their children, Angel was built on the belief that there was a global audience hungry for values-driven storytelling that amplifies light, celebrates hope, and inspires the moral imagination of viewers. That audience became the Angel Guild, a rapidly growing community of 2.6 million paying members who watch, screen, and vote on which films and television series get produced and distributed in theaters and on the Angel app. Angel has achieved the highest audience satisfaction scores in the industry* and the highest average domestic box office per title among all independent studios since 2023. It has done so while evolving a new economic model that shares profits more fully with filmmakers. For more information, visit www.angel.com. Contacts: David Shane Corporate Communications press@angel.com Luk Janssens Investor Relations InvestorRelations@angel.com * www.rottentomatoes.com Popcornmeter (Data sourced April 22, 2026)

title: 7 customizable internal tools for B2B agencies
summary: Compare Airtable, Retool, Softr, Appsmith, monday.com, and Noloco to find the right internal tool for your growing agency's delivery workflows.
body_text: Your account manager built a client tracker in Airtable last spring. Your ops lead built a separate resourcing sheet in a different Airtable base three months later. Somewhere in between, someone spun up a Retool dashboard for finance that nobody outside finance can open. None of these tools talk to each other, and every new hire needs a fifteen minute tour just to find where anything lives. This is what "internal tools" usually looks like at a growing agency: useful pieces, built fast, going in different directions. The fix isn't fewer tools. It's picking one flexible enough to hold client data, project data, and financial data in the same place, without needing an engineer on staff to maintain it. This guide compares seven tools agencies use to build customizable internal tools, ranked on how well they fit agency delivery work specifically (not general internal tooling for a product company), and what each one is genuinely best at. TL;DR The average company now runs 101 apps, and that number just cracked 100 for the first time, according to Okta's 2025 Businesses at Work report . Agencies feel this acutely because every new client can mean another spreadsheet or tool. Airtable, Softr, and Glide are the fastest way to get a working internal tool live, but they were built as app layers, not as a single system of record for a whole agency. Retool and Appsmith are built for engineering teams building internal dashboards, not for non-technical agency owners managing client delivery. monday.com is a strong internal work tracker but treats client access as an add-on, not a first-class feature. Noloco is built specifically to be the operating layer for client-facing service businesses: internal tools, client portals, and permissions in one connected system. What makes an internal tool "customizable" for a B2B agency? A customizable internal tool is software your team builds around your actual delivery process, instead of adapting your process to fit someone else's template. For an agency, that usually means a system that can hold clients, projects, tasks, time, and invoices together, and can be reshaped as your service offering changes. Generic project management software gives you a fixed structure: boards, tickets, or docs. A customizable internal tool gives you a blank data model you configure yourself, which matters because agency delivery rarely looks the same across two clients, let alone two verticals. How do you choose between building and buying an internal tool? Most agencies don't choose once. They start by hacking together a spreadsheet, move to a no-code app layer like Airtable or Softr once volume grows, and eventually hit a ceiling where they need permissions, automations, and a client-facing layer all working together. The decision point is usually volume and stakes: once you're running more than a handful of active clients, or once a client asks to see live status themselves, ad hoc tools stop being safe. That's the moment to compare dedicated platforms rather than stacking another spreadsheet on top of the last one. Which internal tools should growing agencies compare in 2026? Here's a quick-reference view before the detailed breakdown below. Rank Tool Best for 1 Airtable Flexible data layer for teams already comfortable with spreadsheets 2 Softr Fast, simple front ends on top of an existing Airtable base 3 Glide Lightweight mobile-first internal apps 4 Retool Engineering teams building internal dashboards on existing databases 5 Appsmith Open-source, self-hosted internal tools for technical teams 6 monday.com Internal task and workflow tracking for teams that don't need client access 7 Noloco One system for internal tools, client portals, and delivery workflows together ‍ 1. Airtable Airtable is the closest thing to a common language among growing agencies. It's a flexible spreadsheet-database hybrid that most operations leads already know how to use, and a huge share of agency stacks start here for tracking clients, projects, or content calendars. Where it falls short for agency delivery: Airtable's native interfaces weren't built for granular, client-facing permissions, and once an agency needs a real portal (branded, with fields hidden per client), most teams pair it with a front-end layer. Many agencies keep Airtable as the data layer and add an interface on top rather than replacing it. 2. Softr Softr is built to turn an Airtable base into a usable web app fast, which makes it a natural next step once a spreadsheet-based process needs a real interface. It's approachable for non-technical builders and quick to launch. The tradeoff is depth. Softr's permission model and workflow automation are lighter than what agencies need once client portals involve billing, approvals, or multi-step processes, so more complex delivery workflows often outgrow it. 3. Glide Glide specializes in mobile-first internal apps, which suits agencies with field teams or staff who need to log data from a phone rather than a desktop. Setup is quick and the mobile experience is genuinely strong. It's a narrower tool than the others on this list. Glide is a good fit for a single mobile-first use case, but agencies looking for one system to run clients, projects, and finances together will hit its ceiling quickly. 4. Retool Retool is built for engineering teams that need to build internal dashboards and admin panels on top of an existing database quickly. It's powerful in the hands of a developer and widely used inside larger software companies. For most agencies, that's exactly the problem: Retool assumes someone on the team can write queries and manage a technical build. Agencies in the professional services space, per the common ICP profile , typically don't have in-house engineering, which makes Retool a harder fit than a true no-code option. 5. Appsmith Appsmith is an open-source alternative to Retool, popular with technical teams that want to self-host their internal tools rather than pay for a hosted platform. It offers similar dashboard-building capability with more control over deployment. Like Retool, it's designed for developers. Self-hosting also adds ongoing maintenance work, which runs counter to what most agencies actually want: less infrastructure to manage, not more. 6. monday.com monday.com is a mainstream work management tool many agencies already use for internal task tracking, and its visual boards are easy for non-technical teams to adopt. Brand familiarity is a real advantage; most new hires already know how to use it. It was designed for internal team productivity first. Client-facing access is possible but sits on top as an add-on rather than a foundation, and per-seat pricing can get expensive fast as an agency adds external users alongside its internal team. 7. Noloco Noloco is built specifically for growing service businesses that need internal tools and client-facing access to run on the same system, rather than stitching a data layer, a front end, and a client portal together from three different vendors. Agencies already on Airtable can connect it directly and add real interfaces, granular permissions, and automations on top, without migrating data. Redrock Entertainment used Noloco on top of Airtable to run an operating system for more than 100 users, and cut software costs by 60% in the process, according to Jesse VanDenGooy, Technology Solutions Architect at Redrock Entertainment. That's the pattern Noloco is built around: one connected system for the team internally, with client collaboration built in rather than bolted on through a separate portal tool. How do these tools compare on cost, client access, and setup time? Tool Needs coding skills Client-facing portals Granular permissions Built-in automations Airtable ❌ No ⚠️ Limited ⚠️ Limited ⚠️ Basic Softr ❌ No ⚠️ Limited ⚠️ Limited ⚠️ Basic Glide ❌ No ❌ No ⚠️ Limited ⚠️ Basic Retool ✅ Yes ❌ No ✅ Yes ⚠️ Basic Appsmith ✅ Yes ❌ No ✅ Yes ⚠️ Basic monday.com ❌ No ⚠️ Add-on ⚠️ Role-based only ✅ Yes Noloco ❌ No ✅ Yes, included ✅ Field and record level ✅ Yes ‍ How do you decide which tool fits your agency? If your team is a handful of people testing a specific workflow, Airtable, Softr, or Glide will get you there fast without much setup cost. Start there if you're not yet feeling operational pain. If you have engineers on staff and the internal tool never needs to touch a client, Retool or Appsmith give that team full control. That's a rare setup for a professional services firm without in-house IT, though, which is most of this audience. If your agency is past 10 to 15 people, juggling multiple client-facing tools, or fielding requests from clients who want their own visibility into project status, that's the point to look at a platform like Noloco's Agency OS , which combines the interface builder , permissions , and workflow automation agencies need under one system instead of three. Final thoughts Most agencies don't choose an internal tool once. They outgrow one and move to the next, usually at the exact moment a client asks for visibility the current setup can't safely provide. Knowing where each tool's ceiling sits before you build on it saves a migration later. The tools on this list solve real, different problems. Airtable, Softr, and Glide are fast starting points. Retool and Appsmith suit engineering-led teams. monday.com is a solid internal tracker. For agencies that need internal tools and client portals running on the same connected system, that's the specific gap Noloco is built to close. Frequently asked questions What counts as an internal tool for an agency? An internal tool is any custom application a team builds to manage its own operations, such as a client tracker, resourcing dashboard, or approval workflow, rather than software bought off the shelf for a single purpose. Do agencies need developers to build internal tools? Not with no-code platforms. Tools like Airtable, Softr, Glide, and Noloco are designed for non-technical builders, while Retool and Appsmith generally assume someone on the team can write code or queries. Can internal tools also work as client portals? Some can. Airtable and Softr offer limited external sharing, while platforms built around granular permissions, like Noloco, let agencies expose specific fields and records to clients without giving them access to internal data. How long does it take to build a working internal tool? This varies by platform and complexity, but no-code tools generally get a basic version live in days rather than the weeks or months custom development requires. Is it cheaper to build an internal tool or buy a pre-built one? Building gives more control over fit but adds ongoing maintenance time. Pre-built platforms cost more upfront but reduce the time a team spends maintaining and rebuilding tools as the agency's process changes. What happens when an agency outgrows Airtable as its main system? Most agencies either add an interface layer on top of Airtable to keep using it as the data source, or consolidate into a broader operating system once managing multiple disconnected tools becomes the bigger cost. title: Chart of Accounts for SaaS Startups: A 2026 Template
summary: Build a chart of accounts for SaaS that holds up at audit. See revenue segmented for ASC 606, hosting in COGS, and S&M split from G&A.
body_text: What Is a SaaS Chart of Accounts? A SaaS chart of accounts is the master index of every general ledger account, organized into the GAAP financial-statement elements and arranged by a numbering convention so the financials roll up automatically. The conceptual basis for those elements is FASB Concepts Statement No. 6, Elements of Financial Statements , which defines assets, liabilities, equity, revenues, expenses, gains, and losses. Every account in a SaaS COA is, at root, one of those elements. The numbering is just how you keep them in order. What makes a SaaS chart distinct is not the elements but the account-level detail inside them. A software company carries deferred revenue, accrued revenue, and deferred cost of revenue, and almost never carries inventory. Its revenue lines split recurring subscription income from one-time services and usage. Its cost of revenue is dominated by cloud hosting, not raw materials. A generic QuickBooks default template fails the test. It has no deferred revenue account, no hosting COGS line, and a single undifferentiated “Sales” account. As Kruze Consulting frames it, an analyst should be able to read your industry off your chart. Account counts scale with stage. A seed-stage company runs lean at roughly 30 to 40 accounts. By Series A ($1M to $5M ARR) that expands to 50 to 70 with revenue breakouts and COGS detail, and Series B and beyond often reaches 80 to 100 or more once departmental tracking and multi-entity subaccounts come into play, per DualEntry . The structure stays constant. The granularity grows. The SaaS COA Structure The standard SaaS chart of accounts uses a four-digit numbering convention where the first digit identifies the financial-statement class, with accounts running in balance-sheet-first, income-statement-second order. NetSuite, QuickBooks Online, and most mid-market ledgers share this logic. In NetSuite’s own convention , all accounts beginning with 1 are assets, all beginning with 2 are liabilities, and so on, which keeps reporting consistent across periods. QuickBooks Online uses the same four-digit default once account numbers are enabled under Account and Settings, per Intuit . Here is the high-level SaaS chart of accounts template, with the caveat that exact range assignment varies by firm and tool while the classification logic does not. Range Class SaaS-specific accounts 1000-1999 Assets Cash, AR, accrued / unbilled revenue (contract asset), deferred cost of revenue, deferred commissions, capitalized software, fixed assets 2000-2999 Liabilities AP, accrued liabilities, deferred revenue current, deferred revenue long-term, debt 3000-3999 Equity Common stock, preferred, APIC, retained earnings 4000-4999 Revenue Subscription, expansion, usage, setup, professional services, contra-revenue 5000-5999 COGS / Cost of revenue Hosting, embedded third-party software, CS / implementation labor, payment processing, amortization of capitalized software 6000-6999 Operating expense: R&D Engineering wages, dev tools, contractor engineering 7000-7999 Operating expense: S&M Sales wages, commissions, ad spend, marketing tools, events 8000-8999 Operating expense: G&A Exec, finance, HR, legal, rent, insurance, software 9000-9999 Other income / expense, tax Interest, FX, gains and losses, income tax Where a firm draws the lines varies. Some collapse all operating expense into one band, and Kruze uses six-digit numbers with S&M and R&D in adjacent 600000 and 700000 ranges. The number itself is cosmetic. What matters is that each account is correctly classified, because that classification drives gross margin, operating margin, and every benchmark above and below them. Two design rules apply across both tools. First, leave gaps between account numbers so related accounts can be inserted later without renumbering history. If your COGS accounts run 5000 to 5050, start the next at 5100, not 5051. Second, use parent and child subaccounts for discipline rather than a flat sprawl. QuickBooks Online writes this as Hosting:AWS , and NetSuite points a child at its parent via the subaccount field, per the NetSuite chart-of-accounts management guide . SaaS-Specific Application The SaaS accounting structure earns its keep in three account blocks: revenue segmented for ASC 606, COGS that isolates delivery cost, and operating expense split to match SaaS benchmarks. This is where a generic template and a purpose-built one diverge. Revenue accounts (4000s): segment by ARR type, tied to ASC 606 SaaS revenue must be segmented by recognition pattern, because ASC 606 cadence differs by stream and investors compute retention off the breakout. A workable block: 4000 Subscription revenue (recurring, recognized ratably over the contract term) 4100 Expansion / upsell revenue (recurring, separated so you can compute net revenue retention) 4200 Usage / overage revenue (recognized as the usage is incurred) 4300 Implementation / setup revenue (recognized over the period benefited, or at a point in time if a distinct performance obligation) 4400 Professional services revenue (recognized as services are delivered) 4900 Contra-revenue: discounts and refunds Each stream maps to a different ASC 606 treatment, which is why blending them into one “Revenue” account is both an audit and an analytics failure. The AICPA Audit and Accounting Guide: Revenue Recognition devotes Chapter 9 to software entities, walking through when a setup fee is a distinct obligation versus a material right. The reason expansion revenue gets its own account is metrics, not aesthetics. Net revenue retention is (beginning ARR minus churned minus contraction plus expansion) divided by beginning ARR, excluding new-customer revenue, per ChartMogul . Gross revenue retention strips out expansion and caps at 100%. If new, expansion, and base subscription all land in one account, neither number can be computed from the ledger. That metric only exists if the COA was built to produce it. COGS accounts (5000s): isolate the cost of delivering the product SaaS cost of revenue is the single largest lever on gross margin, so the COGS block must capture every cost tied to delivering the product and nothing else. The rule is mechanical. If a cost is incurred to deliver the running product to existing customers, it is COGS. If it is incurred to build, sell, or run the company, it is operating expense, per The SaaS CFO . A SaaS COGS block: 5000 Hosting and cloud infrastructure (AWS, GCP, Azure production environments) 5100 Third-party software embedded in the product (data, monitoring, security APIs that ship inside the product) 5200 Customer success and implementation labor (the delivery headcount, not post-sale account management that is really sales) 5300 Payment processing fees (Stripe and similar, where you are the merchant of record) 5400 Professional services COGS (labor to deliver paid services revenue) 5500 Amortization of capitalized software (the periodic charge on internally developed software) The consequence of getting this wrong is direct. SaaS gross margins benchmark at 71 to 72% on a blended basis, with the strongest companies above 80%, per the High Alpha / OpenView SaaS Benchmarks . Drop hosting into operating expense and your gross margin reads artificially high, which dies in diligence. Drop a sales commission into COGS and your margin reads artificially low. Both distortions survive only until someone who knows SaaS reads the statements. Operating expense accounts (6000s to 8000s): split S&M, R&D, G&A Operating expense must split into R&D, S&M, and G&A, with Customer Success sitting in COGS or G&A depending on whether the function delivers the product or manages the account. The split is not optional for a company that reports against benchmarks. The R&D bucket (6000s) carries engineering wages, dev tooling, and contractor engineering, and it matters beyond reporting. Domestic engineering wages are the core of the qualified research expense base, and software development is treated as Section 174 research expenditure. New Section 174A permanently restored immediate expensing of domestic R&E for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, while foreign R&E still amortizes over 15 years, per Grant Thornton . A chart that cleanly isolates domestic engineering wages makes both the credit calculation and the 174A treatment far easier to support, which is exactly why Indinero’s business tax services treat the COA design and the return as one workflow. S&M (7000s) holds sales wages, commissions, advertising, and events. Capitalized commissions under ASC 340-40 sit on the balance sheet as a deferred cost asset, not here, with only the amortization flowing through. G&A (8000s) covers executive, finance, HR, and legal wages, rent, insurance, and general software. S&M must be separated from G&A because the magic number, CAC payback, and the Rule of 40 are all computed off isolated sales and marketing spend. Lump S&M into a generic SG&A account and none of those numbers can be pulled from the ledger. The same data feeds your board reporting, which is why fractional CFO advisory and the COA design belong in the same engagement. Common Pitfalls The recurring SaaS chart-of-accounts mistakes are predictable, and most trace back to using a generic template instead of a SaaS-built one. Each one distorts a number that someone in diligence will eventually reclassify. Hosting in operating expense instead of COGS. AWS and GCP production spend is cost of revenue. Put it in OpEx and your reported gross margin inflates, then evaporates the moment a diligence team moves it, per The SaaS CFO . The consequence is a margin that fails due diligence. No expansion-versus-new revenue separation. One blended revenue account makes NRR, GRR, and NDR impossible to compute from the ledger, per ChartMogul . The consequence is broken retention analysis the night before a board meeting. Sales commissions misclassified as COGS. Commissions are a selling expense, not a cost of delivering the product, per DualEntry . The consequence is inflated COGS and deflated gross margin. No deferred revenue account. Collecting annual prepayments without a deferred revenue liability recognizes revenue prematurely. The consequence is a clear ASC 606 violation and an audit red flag. No current-versus-long-term split on deferred revenue. A single deferred revenue account obscures the within-12-months versus beyond-12-months presentation auditors expect. The consequence is an audit finding on balance-sheet classification. S&M lumped with G&A. The consequence is dead magic-number, CAC-payback, and Rule of 40 analysis, because all three are computed off isolated S&M. Over-granular accounts nobody maintains. A 200-account chart that gets miscoded is worse than a 60-account chart coded correctly, per Kruze Consulting . The consequence is a chart that drifts and reclassification work after a tax period closes. Most generalist firms miss these until an auditor flags them. Indinero’s books are audit-ready by default, because GAAP discipline is baked into how the team operates, not added later. The CPA team catches the misclassification during monthly close review, before it reaches a data room. The Audit-Ready Standard An audit-ready SaaS chart of accounts is one where the financial statements roll up directly from the ledger with no off-system reclassification, every ASC 606 contract liability and contract asset is presented per ASC 606-10-45-1 through -3, and the revenue and cost segmentation serves both GAAP and the SaaS metrics in one structure. In practice, three things hold true. First, classification matches the standards. Deferred revenue is a contract liability presented net per ASC 606-10-45-1, split current and long-term. Contract assets are presented separately from receivables per ASC 606-10-45-3. Capitalized commissions sit as deferred costs under ASC 340-40, and capitalized development as an intangible under ASC 350-40, each with amortization flowing to the right line. Second, the chart was built before the transactions, not reverse-engineered after. The expensive version of this work is recategorizing historical transactions, which gets genuinely painful once a tax period has closed. Series A audit prep should be months of clean books, not weeks of scramble to reclassify two years of miscoded hosting spend. Our audit preparation walkthrough covers what that readiness looks like in practice. Third, the same chart serves GAAP and the board deck. Revenue segmented for ASC 606 is the same segmentation that produces NRR and GRR. Cost isolated for gross margin is the same data the Rule of 40 needs. When the COA is built once, correctly, the audit, the tax return, the R&D credit base, and the investor metrics all draw from one source of truth. Build it right the first time. How indinero Approaches the SaaS COA Indinero’s CPA team builds the SaaS chart of accounts inside the tooling you already run, then maintains it as part of monthly close. The structure above is not a one-time setup deliverable. It is a living chart that has to stay correct every month as new revenue streams, products, and entities appear, which is where most internally maintained charts drift. The GAAP discipline is handled upfront, so your month-end close runs in roughly 5 days instead of 45, and your audit prep is months of clean books instead of weeks of scramble. The SaaS COA is the foundation of that. Revenue segmented for ASC 606, hosting seated in COGS, S&M separated from G&A, and deferred revenue split current and long-term, all built and maintained so the statements roll up clean. There is no platform to migrate to. Indinero builds and maintains the chart of accounts inside QuickBooks Online or NetSuite, integrating with the stack you already use, with no proprietary lock-in. The accounting services scope covers the full monthly GAAP-compliant close, financial statement preparation across the P&L, balance sheet, cash flow, and statement of equity, cash-to-accrual conversion, multi-entity consolidation, ASC 606 revenue recognition, and audit prep and support. The structural difference from a tool-only or bench-style provider is that the chart is built by CPAs and bundled with tax and fractional CFO under one monthly engagement. The same team that designs the revenue segmentation knows it has to feed the R&D credit base and the Section 174A treatment, because the same engagement files the return. Indinero has run continuously since 2009 under stable ownership, holds a 5-star Clutch rating, serves 500+ regular customers, is SOC 2 compliant (2026), and offers month-to-month engagements with pricing that starts at $750/mo. For a growth-stage SaaS company heading into a Series A audit, the question is rarely whether you have a chart of accounts. It is whether the one you have was built to survive scrutiny. If you want a SaaS COA built right from day one, reach out for a free consultation . We’d love to learn about your business and find where we can help. Frequently asked questions Founders and finance leaders ask the same questions when they sit down to structure or restructure a SaaS chart of accounts. The answers below are grounded in the structure above and the work Indinero’s CPA team does building and maintaining audit-ready charts of accounts for growth-stage SaaS companies inside QuickBooks Online and NetSuite. Why do SaaS companies need a different chart of accounts than a traditional services business? A SaaS chart of accounts carries deferred revenue, accrued revenue, deferred cost of revenue, and hosting COGS that a traditional services COA never needs. Software revenue splits recurring subscription from one-time services and usage, and cost of revenue is dominated by cloud hosting rather than raw materials or inventory. An analyst should be able to read your business model straight off the chart, which a generic QuickBooks default template with one undifferentiated Sales account cannot deliver. How granular should revenue accounts be in a SaaS COA? SaaS revenue should be segmented by recognition pattern, typically subscription, expansion, usage, implementation, professional services, and a contra-revenue line. Each stream maps to a different ASC 606 treatment, so blending them into one Revenue account is both an audit failure and an analytics failure. Expansion needs its own account specifically so net revenue retention and gross revenue retention can be computed directly from the ledger. That metric only exists if the COA was built to produce it. Should hosting costs go in COGS or operating expenses? Hosting and cloud infrastructure for production environments belong in COGS, because they are a direct cost of delivering the running product to existing customers. The rule is mechanical. If a cost is incurred to deliver the product, it is cost of revenue, and if it is incurred to build, sell, or run the company, it is operating expense. Drop hosting into OpEx and your gross margin reads artificially high, then evaporates the moment a diligence team reclassifies it. How do I structure S&M, R&D, and G&A for SaaS-style operating expense reporting? Split operating expense into R&D, S&M, and G&A, and place Customer Success in COGS or G&A based on its role. R&D carries engineering wages, dev tooling, and contractor engineering. S&M holds sales wages, commissions, advertising, and events. G&A covers exec, finance, HR, legal, rent, and insurance. Keeping S&M isolated from G&A is what makes the magic number, CAC payback, and Rule of 40 computable from the ledger. When should I add departmental tags or classes to the COA? Add departmental tags or classes once you need expense reporting by function or entity that account numbering alone cannot capture. That inflection usually arrives around Series B, as the chart reaches 80 to 100 accounts. Seed-stage companies run lean at 30 to 40 accounts, and Series A expands to 50 to 70 with revenue and COGS detail. The structure stays constant while granularity grows. Add tags before the sprawl, not after, so departmental P&L rolls up without manual reclassification. How do I avoid breaking historical comparability when I restructure the COA? Leave numbering gaps between accounts so related lines insert later without renumbering history, and use parent and child subaccounts instead of a flat sprawl. If your COGS accounts run 5000 to 5050, start the next band at 5100, not 5051. Restructuring after a tax period has closed means recategorizing historical transactions, which is the expensive version of this work. Indinero’s CPA team builds the chart before the transactions and maintains it during monthly close, so prior periods stay comparable. Does QuickBooks Online or NetSuite affect how I structure the COA? QuickBooks Online and NetSuite share the same four-digit numbering logic, so the classification structure of a SaaS COA stays identical across both tools. NetSuite assigns all 1-series accounts to assets and 2-series to liabilities, and QuickBooks Online uses the same four-digit default once account numbers are enabled. Subaccount syntax differs, with QuickBooks writing Hosting:AWS and NetSuite pointing a child at its parent. Indinero builds and maintains the chart inside whichever you already run, with no proprietary platform to migrate to.

body_text: The Canterbury Park Hall of Fame will induct three new members in a ceremony to be held Friday, July 24 as part of Hall of Fame Weekend at the Shakopee, Minn. racetrack. The Class of 2026 includes thoroughbred owner and breeder Pete Mattson, all-time leading money earning Minnesota-bred quarter horse Dickey Bob and former chief veterinarian and Minnesota Racing Commission chair Dr. Camille McArdle. The three join a group of more than 50 individuals and horses that comprise the best of Minnesota horse racing. The green “MHC” silks of Mattson’s stable combine two important facets of his life – his business and horse racing. Carried to victory by Minnesota-bred stakes winners Fireman Oscar, Doctor Pete Mattson and Jareth Loveberry Oscar, Astronaut Oscar, Retired Kathy, Molly’s Angel, Thealligatorhunter, Summer Winner and more, the biggest days at Canterbury Park were some of the best for Mattson. From his first win with a partnership in 1991 with Wild Moose Chase, to solo-owned winner Dazzle Baby in 2002, to an exciting debut win by home-bred Mighty Samurai in 2026, Mattson’s support and success at Canterbury spans more than three decades. Dickey Bob Dickey Bob’s first win as a 2-year-old and his final win at the age of 10 both came at Canterbury Park. There were 30 additional wins in between at multiple tracks for the son of Apollitical Jess at distances ranging from 110 yards to 400 yards. Out of the mare Paint or More, Dickey Bob is the richest of seven full siblings who combined earned nearly $1.5 million. Owned and bred by Bruce and Judy Lunderborg’s Lunderborg LLC, Dickey Bob retired last year and is living on trainer Jason Olmstead’s farm. His $529,119 in earnings over 70 races is the most ever by a Minnesota-bred quarter horse. In 1985, Dr. McArdle was named the MRC’s first chief veterinarian for the fledgling industry. She built the veterinary department around these core principles: protecting horses’ health and the integrity of the sport. In 1993, Dr. McArdle was appointed to the Racing Commission during a time of transition. She provided steady leadership after the closure of Canterbury Downs at the end of 1992, then helped guide the sport into a new era with the opening of Canterbury Park in 1994. Serving under five governors over 41 years, she was named commission chair in 2021. Dr. McArdle resigned from the commission in 2025 after state government officials rejected her efforts to help Canterbury Park and Running Aces add new sources of purse revenue. Dr. McArdle The Canterbury Park Hall of Fame was founded in 1995 to recognize people and horses that have made important and lasting contributions to the racing industry within the state. The selection committee consists of representatives of local horsemen organizations, media, and Canterbury Park.

title: IMG Appoints Jackie Stevenson as Chief Client & Operations Officer
summary: Global sports marketing agency IMG today announced it has appointed Jackie Stevenson into the newly created role of Chief Client & Operations Officer. The appointment is part of the centralised leadership structure IMG unveiled in April, strengthening how the company…
body_text: N e w s Return to News Jul 7, 2026 IMG IMG Appoints Jackie Stevenson as Chief Client & Operations Officer Global sports marketing agency IMG today announced it has appointed Jackie Stevenson into the newly created role of Chief Client & Operations Officer. The appointment is part of the centralised leadership structure IMG unveiled in April, strengthening how the company helps more than 250 rightsholders and partners accelerate growth, deepen fan engagement and unlock greater commercial value in an increasingly complex sports and entertainment landscape. Reporting to IMG President Adam Kelly, Stevenson will lead client delivery and operations globally, ensuring IMG’s expertise is deployed seamlessly across markets while creating a more connected operating model for clients. She will bring together IMG’s consulting, media rights, brand partnerships, production, digital, data and event management capabilities to help partners unlock greater commercial impact through integrated solutions. Stevenson brings more than three decades of experience helping global organisations accelerate growth through strategy, innovation, transformation and operational leadership. Most recently Global Chief Strategy & Innovation Officer at M+C Saatchi, she has built and scaled international businesses across marketing, media, sport and entertainment. She co-founded The Brooklyn Brothers, growing it into an internationally recognised agency before its acquisition by IPG, where she went on to hold a group leadership position overseeing growth across multiple markets. Kelly said: “Jackie brings exceptional experience leading growth and transformation across complex global organisations. She has operated at scale, built and integrated businesses, and understands what it takes to deliver for multi-market partners. Her appointment is a key step in strengthening how IMG operates as one connected organisation, delivering integrated solutions and long-term value for partners.” Stevenson said: “Sport and entertainment are evolving faster than ever, and clients increasingly need integrated partners who can connect rights, content, technology, data and commercial expertise. IMG is uniquely positioned to do that at global scale and I’m excited to help shape the next chapter with Adam, Barney and the brilliant teams across the business.” The appointment follows IMG’s announcement in April that Barney Francis was named Chief Business Officer, bringing together the company’s commercial functions under a single integrated go-to-market approach. Together, these two new leadership roles further strengthen the connection between IMG’s commercial, client and operational functions.

title: Mastering Instagram's For You Page (FYP): A Comprehensive Guide
summary: Instagram algorithm got you down? Not to worry: we demystify the Instagram For You Page in this comprehensive guide.
body_text: Welcome to our comprehensive guide on mastering Instagram's For You Page (FYP). What is the Instagram For You Page? The Instagram For You Page is a feature that shows users personalized content based on their past interactions with the app. It differs from the Explore page, which displays popular content globally using various criteria such as viral posts and trending topics. To curate content for the For You Page, Instagram uses a sophisticated algorithm that accounts for the user's search history, interaction with other users, use of hashtags, and the type of content they enjoy viewing. The algorithm then shows the user a wide range of content, including posts, videos, and stories, that they might find interesting. Benefits of Mastering the For You Page The For You Page is a powerful tool that can benefit anyone looking to increase their presence and engagement on Instagram. Mastering the For You Page can help individuals and businesses alike reach a wider audience, improve their content strategy, and ultimately grow their brand. Later in this article, we'll explore the benefits of mastering the For You Page and provide tips for creating content that resonates with your target audience. Having your content featured on the For You Page can significantly increase your reach and engagement as it exposes your content to a wider audience that is already interested in your niche. Understanding the Instagram For You Page Algorithm The Instagram For You Page (FYP) is an algorithm-driven feed that displays personalized content to users based on their interests, preferences, and previous engagement on the platform. It's a powerful tool for discovering new content and connecting with like-minded individuals. To outrank other websites and gain prominence on the FYP, it is crucial to understand the factors that influence the algorithm. Here are some key aspects to consider: 1. User Engagement User engagement plays a vital role in determining the visibility of your content on the FYP. The algorithm takes into account various metrics such as likes, comments, saves, shares, and video views. To boost engagement, create captivating content that resonates with your target audience. Encourage meaningful interactions by asking questions, utilizing calls-to-action, and responding promptly to comments. 2. Relevance and Interest The FYP algorithm assesses the relevance of your content to each user's interests. It analyzes the topics, hashtags, and accounts that users frequently engage with and tailors their feed accordingly. To increase your chances of appearing on the FYP, conduct thorough research on your target audience's preferences and incorporate relevant hashtags and trending topics in your posts. 3. Content Freshness Instagram values fresh and up-to-date content. Regularly posting new and engaging content signals to the algorithm that you are an active user and increases your visibility. Establish a consistent posting schedule that aligns with your audience's online activity and strive to deliver high-quality content consistently. 4. Post Performance The performance of your posts, including the engagement they receive shortly after being published, is crucial for FYP visibility. The algorithm closely monitors the initial response to your content and determines whether it should be shown to a broader audience. Encourage early engagement by promoting your posts within your existing network and utilizing Instagram's interactive features such as stickers and polls. Include relevant keywords in your bio to increase the chances of appearing in search results. 2. Create Engaging and High-Quality Content To captivate your audience and encourage engagement, focus on creating visually appealing and high-quality content. Factors such as engagement rate, user interactions, and post frequency also play a vital role in the algorithm's decision-making process. This is where having a content strategy in place can help you stay ahead of the game. It's important to stay up to date with new algorithm updates. Types of Content and Formats to Consider Instagram's For You Page offers a great opportunity to reach a wider audience and boost engagement levels. title: HR Pulse: How to Create a Resume That Passes AI Screening and Still Sounds Like You
summary: In this article, we break down common myths about AI screening, explain why strong resumes still get filtered out, and outline practical ways to create a CV that works for both technology and people.
body_text: Employers are increasingly looking for resumes that balance the right format, targeted keywords, measurable achievements, and a mix of hard and soft skills that match the role. Creating an AI-friendly resume does not mean letting AI do all the work for you. AI tools can help job seekers move faster but overusing them can lead to resumes that sound generic, rely too heavily on keywords, or fail to reflect the candidate’s real strengths and voice. The goal is not to ‘beat the system.’ It is to build a resume that is decipherable by technology and convincing to people. In this article, we break down common myths about AI screening, explain why strong resumes still get filtered out, and outline practical ways to create a CV that works for both technology and people. To understand how AI really affects hiring decisions, it helps to clear up a few common misconceptions. Myth 1: AI automatically rejects resumes Reality: Resumes are filtered out when they are unclear, misaligned, or when application questions are answered incorrectly, not because an algorithm “rejected” the candidate . Section 1: Making Your Resume Stand Out in the Age of AI: Formatting and Tailoring Tips As AI-powered tools and Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) play a larger role in the hiring process, job seekers need to be more intentional about how they present their experience. The right formatting and a tailored approach ensure both the technology and the humans behind the process can clearly understand your qualifications. Here’s how candidates can make their resumes stand out Use Clean, ATS-Friendly Formatting AI systems work best with simple, consistent resume structures. Clear section headers such as work experience, skills, and education help parsing tools identify key information quickly. Candidates should avoid text boxes, columns, graphics, and decorative elements that many systems struggle to interpret. Myth 2: Creative designs impress AI Reality: Most screening tools prioritize structure over style. Visual elements such as tables, graphics, or text boxes can confuse and interrupt how information is parsed. A simple, conventional layout helps ensure your experience is captured accurately before a recruiter ever sees it. Standard, readable fonts, like Arial, Calibri, or Times New Roman, are recommended, and saving your resume as a Word (.docx) file is often recommended for maximum compatibility, however many systems also accept well-structured PDFs. Important details, including contact information and job titles, should always appear in the main body of the resume, not in headers or footers. Simple bullet points are easier for AI to read than decorative symbols, and traditional chronological or hybrid formats remain the most effective. Creative or overly visual layouts may appeal to the eye but can be misread, or skipped entirely, by screening tools. Tailor Your Resume to Each Job Description In the age of AI screening, tailoring a resume isn’t optional, it is one of the most effective ways to move forward in the hiring process. Modern ATS and AI tools compare resumes directly with the job description, scanning for key skills, terminology, and experience. When a resume naturally incorporates the same language used in the posting, it’s more likely to pass initial filters. Tailoring also helps candidates highlight their most relevant strengths. By adjusting bullet points and emphasizing accomplishments that align with the role, applicants make it easier for both automated systems and hiring managers to see why they are a strong fit. This approach keeps the resume focused, reduces irrelevant information, and signals genuine interest in the specific position. Section 2: Why Some Resumes Don’t Make It Past AI Screening Even with strong experience and good intentions, many resumes fail not because of substance, but because of how they are interpreted by screening systems. If you have been applying to jobs and hearing little to nothing back, the issue may not be your qualifications, it may be how your resume is being processed. Today's ATSs and AI-powered tools don’t read resumes like humans do; instead, they scan for specific keywords, structure, and data points. If your resume isn’t aligned with how these systems work, it can be filtered out within seconds. One of the most common reasons resumes are rejected is the lack of relevant keywords. AI tools are designed to match resumes to job descriptions, so if your resume doesn’t include the same terminology such as specific skills, tools, or job titles it may not rank high enough to move forward. Even if your experience is strong, using different phrasing from what appears in the job description can cause the system to overlook your qualifications. Myth 3: More keywords always improve your chances Reality: Overuse of keywords can actually hurt your resume. AI screening tools look for context and relevance, not repetition. Keywords work best when they are naturally embedded in clear results, focused experience that aligns with the role. Another issue may be unclear or non-traditional structure. As mentioned previously, AI systems are programmed to recognize standard resume sections such as work experience, education, and skills. When these headings are replaced with more creative titles, the system may struggle to categorize your information correctly. This can impact how your resume is ranked, even if the content itself is strong. Ultimately, getting rejected doesn’t always mean you do not have the qualifications. More often, it means your resume isn’t optimized for how AI evaluates candidates. By understanding how these systems work, you can better position your experience to be seen, understood, and moved forward in the hiring process. Section 3: Level up! What Makes a CV AI-Friendly Understanding why resumes fall short is the first step. The next is applying that insight to deliberately strengthen how your experience is presented. Leveling up your resume today is less about adding more, and more about presenting your experience more clearly, strategically, and with impact. One of the most effective ways to improve your resume is by using AI tools to better understand how your experience is being presented. It is important to find the right balance between being AI friendly and appealing to what a recruiter is actually looking for. Your resume should be clear, relevant, and still feel authentic to you. Myth 4: Using AI guarantees a stronger resume Reality: AI improves efficiency, not judgment. AI can help draft, refine, and tailor content, but resumes perform best when candidates review, personalize, and validate every line to ensure accuracy, credibility, and authentic voice. Focus on results, not just responsibilities Metrics are highly valued by both AI systems and recruiters, so highlighting outcomes such as percentages, growth, or efficiency improvements can significantly strengthen your resume. Even small contributions can help show value when framed the right way. Here’s what that difference can look like in practice: Before: Responsible for onboarding new employees. After: Improved employee onboarding completion rates by 30% by redesigning training materials and delivery format. Before: Assisted with event planning. After: Supported planning and execution of five campus events attended by 250+ participants, coordinating logistics and communications. Use AI as a support, not a shortcut. Use specific language to explain what you have done and how you have done it, including the systems or technologies involved. While AI can help polish and structure your resume, it should never create experience, exaggerate results, or make decisions on your behalf. Be intentional, not automated. It’s understandable to want to apply quickly to many roles, but mass application tools can work against you. Many employers can spot automated submissions and deprioritize them. Focusing instead on roles that genuinely interest you, and applying thoughtfully, often leads to better response rates and more meaningful conversations. At the end of the day, an AI friendly resume is not about gaming the system. It is about presenting your experience in a way that is easy for technology to read and compelling for a recruiter to move forward. Self-Assessment: Is Your Resume AI Aware and Human ready? Here is a checklist you can run through before applying for your next position. It is designed to help you evaluate clarity, credibility, and alignment, and to avoid using only keyword coverage. 1. Structure & Readability I have used standard section headings (e.g., Work experience, skills, education). My resume follows a simple, single column layout. Important details, contact info, job titles, dates, appear in the main body and not in the headers or footers. 2. Relevance & Language My resume reflects the language used in the job description without copying it directly. I describe my experience using specific tools, systems, or processes where applicable. My skills section reinforces what is shown in my experience without duplication. 3. Impact & Credibility Bullet points show outcomes, results, or improvements. Any metrics I include are accurate and justifiable. My descriptions explain what I actually contributed, not only a team or department mandate. 4. AI Use & Authenticity If I used AI tools, I reviewed and edited the language to match my voice. No bullet point feels vague, inflated, or disconnected from my real experience. I can confidently explain every line in an interview. 5. Final Check If AI screening were not involved, this resume would still clearly tell my story. A recruiter could understand my role, value, and strengths in under one minute. Note: This self-assessment is designed as a reflective tool, to help job seekers balance AI screening requirements with clear ‑human-centered‑ storytelling. “ Just as resumes today are read by both technology and people, the most effective candidates are those who design for both without losing their voice.” Human Experience, Strategically Presented AI is changing the job search, but the fundamentals of a strong resume still matter. Clear formatting, relevant keywords, measurable accomplishments, strong contact information, and a thoughtful mix of hard and soft skills can all improve the chances that your resume is successfully parsed and seriously considered. A resume summary and tailored language can also help show alignment with the role without sacrificing clarity. As AI becomes a standard part of hiring, the resumes that stand out will be those that pair thoughtful optimization with genuine voice. Job seekers who succeed will be intentional in how they tailor their materials, using AI as a support, while staying firmly in control of their story, tone, and credibility. Empower your future and transform your ideas into impactful solutions.
